title: Living ashtpadi 15
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 16, salok: no form, no color

cards: Listen to two Sikhs meet. One says: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa. The other answers: Waheguru ji ki Fateh.
The Khalsa belongs to Waheguru; the victory belongs to Waheguru. It's a greeting heard at doors, on phones, at the end of speeches. And look at what it does.
Every time two people meet, they hand the victory away. Whatever either of them has won, or is about to win, isn't theirs. That might sound like a recipe for feeling weak.

teach.b: This week the fifteenth ashtpadi said three things. God is brimful of every power. God knows every pain.

And nothing is done on our own; it's all soaked in His color. You might expect the result to be passivity: if all the power is God's, why bother? In Sikh life, the result has been something like the reverse.

Take the Fateh greeting. Sikh memory tells of early Khalsa Sikhs who were outnumbered, poor and hunted, and who said it anyway. In that telling, handing the victory to Waheguru didn't make them give up.
It let them stand up, because their courage didn't depend on how strong they felt that morning.
The Ardas, the standing prayer, has a string of names for God that make the same point: nimaaniaan de maan, nitaaniaan de taan, nioteaan dee ot.
Honor of the dishonored, strength of the strengthless, shelter of the shelterless. Taan is strength. Nitaan is someone without it.
And the One is called the strength of exactly those people. Here's the turn: strength borrowed is still strength.

teach.h: SAP FROM THE SOIL IS STILL SAP.
teach.b: A tree's sap comes up from the soil, and nobody says the tree is weak. A lamp's light comes down the wire, and it still lights the room.
In this picture, asking for strength rather than manufacturing it doesn't make a person less able. It makes them able in a way that doesn't run out when they do.
That's why chardi kalaa, rising spirits, can survive a bad day. And asking for strength isn't a sign that you've failed. In this tradition, it's the normal way strength arrives.

how: Sikhs greet each other with Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh, giving the victory to God, and the Ardas calls God the strength of the strengthless; Sukhmani's fifteenth ashtpadi lies behind both thoughts.

o: a shelter for those with no home
strength, the power to stand and act
pride in one's own past victories

s: the Fateh greeting gives the victory to Waheguru, not to the speakers
Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh.
asking for strength shows you've failed
in this tradition it's the normal way strength arrives.
believing all power is God's has made Sikhs passive
Sikh history suggests the reverse: courage that didn't depend on feeling strong.

games.q: you're dreading a hard conversation and feel too weak for it. what does living ashtpadi 15 suggest?
o: ask for strength, then go and do it.
skip it; it's in God's hands.
games.why: ask, then act. the Ardas calls the One the strength of the strengthless, and strength borrowed is still strength.

practice: Think of one thing today you don't feel strong enough for, a conversation, a task, just getting through the afternoon, and instead of bracing, try asking.

If you pray, ask Waheguru plainly, in your own words, for the strength you need. If you don't, breathe in as if strength could arrive on the breath, from somewhere deeper than you, and let it come without gripping.

wordCard.voice: Taan, strength. The One is called the strength of the strengthless, and strength borrowed from the Giver is still strength.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: taan, strength; in the Ardas the One is nitaaniaan de taan, strength of the strengthless.

carryVoice: Your line: borrowed strength. Sap from the soil is still sap. That's day four hundred ninety-seven, done.
